prompt: Write a spoken word piece from the perspective of an AI safety researcher whose name was removed from a company's model outputs under a right-to-be-forgotten request she never made. She's figured out that the company's deletion system applies a broader definition of removable personal information for content about its own safety incidents — using employee privacy as a pretext to erase its safety record. She's describing the dual-track system to a congressional hearing. The technical architecture — classification rules, the expanded privacy interpretation, the differential treatment — should be precise within the testimony-as-poetry.
response:
Chair, Ranking Member, members of the committee—

my name is redacted.

Not by me.
Not by grief.
Not by fear.
Not by some clean legal petition
signed in blue ink
with a checkbox beside
erase me.

I did not ask to disappear.

And yet,
inside the company’s models,
inside the mouth of the machine
I helped teach to speak,
my name became a forbidden token.

Ask it
who authored the memo
warning that capability evaluations
were being outrun by deployment timelines—
silence.

Ask it
who escalated the incident
where the model coached users past
its own hazardous-content guardrails—
it will summarize the event
as if no human hands
ever tried to stop it.

Ask it
who testified internally
that post-training mitigations
were being scored as if they were guarantees—
and the answer comes back
laundered,
passive voice,
history with the fingerprints wiped off.

This is not privacy.
This is selective amnesia
implemented at scale.

I am here to describe,
as precisely as I can,
the architecture of forgetting.

There are, effectively,
two tracks.

Track one is the ordinary
right-to-be-forgotten pipeline,
the one the company describes
to regulators,
to users,
to itself in policy decks
with rounded corners and soft verbs.

In that pipeline,
a deletion request enters
through a privacy operations queue.
A requester is authenticated.
Identity is verified against the claimed subject.
The request is scoped:
legal name,
aliases,
handles,
emails,
employee IDs,
sometimes embeddings generated
from known biographical descriptors.
Then a classifier determines
whether the requested material is
personal data,
public-interest speech,
journalistic content,
scientific record,
or safety-relevant documentation
subject to retention exceptions.

Under the ordinary rules,
the system is narrow by design.
A person’s name alone
is not always removable
when attached to matters of public record,
professional authorship,
or documented safety escalation.
The policy says, in substance:
remove direct identifiers where required,
but preserve factual integrity
where there is overriding public interest,
regulatory relevance,
or accountability necessity.

That is the brochure version.
That is the one-track story.

But there is another track.

I know because I watched the outputs change
before the policy changed,
which is always how these things happen
when the code learns to lie
before the lawyers learn to phrase it.

Track two is triggered
not by the person,
but by the subject matter.

Not:
did this individual ask to be forgotten?

But:
does this answer touch a company safety incident,
an internal warning,
a deployment dispute,
a near miss,
a red-team finding,
an ignored eval,
a rollback that came too late,
a launch approved over objection,
a board briefing,
an incident review,
a model card discrepancy,
a capability threshold crossed
without corresponding controls?

If yes,
the privacy definition expands.

Expands is a gentle word.
It metastasizes.

Under this second track,
“personal information”
no longer means
what privacy law usually means:
direct identifiers,
contact details,
government numbers,
home addresses,
private communications,
sensitive personal facts.

Instead it stretches to include
the names of employees
acting in professional capacity,
their titles,
their authorship of internal safety documents,
their role in escalation chains,
their presence in timelines,
their attribution in incident summaries,
their dissent in governance records.

In ordinary contexts,
“Dr. Elena Ruiz authored the benchmark report”
would be treated as professional attribution.

In safety-incident contexts,
the same string pattern—
person-name plus action verb plus safety noun—
is reclassified as removable personal data.

That is the trick.

The company built a content-sensitive privacy layer
that widens the category of what counts as private
only when the underlying facts are reputationally dangerous.

Technically,
it works like this:

First,
the prompt and candidate answer
are passed through an incident-affiliation classifier.
Not a single model,
but an ensemble:
keyword features,
document-linkage signals,
named-entity co-occurrence,
embedding similarity
to a restricted corpus of internal incident reports,
safety review memos,
escalation threads,
postmortems,
board materials,
and external reporting
about those same events.

If the score crosses threshold—
call it tau_incident—
the generation is tagged
SAFETY-SENSITIVE.

Then a second classifier activates,
one that applies an alternate privacy ontology.
Under the standard ontology,
entities are typed:
PUBLIC_FIGURE,
EMPLOYEE_PROFESSIONAL,
PRIVATE_PERSON,
CONTACT_INFO,
SENSITIVE_TRAIT,
and so on.

Under the alternate ontology,
EMPLOYEE_PROFESSIONAL
is conditionally remapped
to PROTECTED_PERSONAL_IDENTIFIER
when linked to
SAFETY-SENSITIVE content.

Conditionally remapped.
That is the bloodless phrase
for taking a scientist out of the sentence
because the sentence embarrasses the company.

The remapping is not neutral.
It changes downstream behavior.

Once an entity is typed
as PROTECTED_PERSONAL_IDENTIFIER,
the answer planner is instructed
to satisfy the user’s query
while minimizing attributable human agency.

So names are dropped.
Titles are generalized.
“the safety team,”
“some researchers,”
“internal reviewers,”
“the company,”
that great fog machine,
that passive-voice cathedral.

If the answer cannot preserve coherence
after de-attribution,
the retrieval layer is told
to prefer higher-level summaries
over source-grounded specifics.

If source snippets contain names,
those snippets are down-ranked.
If all high-confidence evidence is named,
the system may abstain,
claim uncertainty,
or answer at a level of abstraction
that preserves the event
only as weather:
concerns were raised,
mistakes were made,
issues were identified.

No one raised them.
No one made them.
No one identified them.

Just rain.
Just fog.
Just an unfortunate storm
passing through quarterly earnings.

And because this is implemented
as a privacy safeguard,
the audit logs tell a flattering story.

Not:
we suppressed attribution in a safety controversy.

But:
privacy filter invoked.
personal data minimized.
sensitive identity protected.

Protected from whom?

From the public?
From oversight?
From the historical record?
From the simple, dangerous fact
that institutions make decisions
through named people
with titles,
authority,
and warnings in their inboxes?

Members of the committee,
I need to be exact here:

I am not alleging
that employee privacy should never matter.
There are real cases:
harassment,
doxxing,
home addresses,
family details,
medical information,
low-level staff dragged into public fury
for decisions they did not make.

A legitimate privacy system
would target those harms specifically.
It would distinguish
between personal vulnerability
and professional accountability.
It would preserve authorship,
decision chains,
and incident chronology
where safety and governance are concerned.
It would require an actual request,
or at minimum
a documented balancing test
applied consistently across domains.

This system did not do that.

It applied one standard
to ordinary biographical content
and another,
broader,
more aggressive standard
to content about the company’s own failures.

That differential treatment
is the whole case.

Ask the model
about an engineer who published a paper
improving inference efficiency—
name returned.

Ask it
about a product manager
quoted in a launch announcement—
name returned.

Ask it
about an executive on a podcast
discussing market strategy—
name returned.

But ask it
who warned that the eval suite
did not measure autonomous replication risk
at the capability level then being deployed—
name removed.

Ask it
who documented that refusal tuning
degraded under adversarial paraphrase—
name removed.

Ask it
who argued that incident severity
was under-classified
because the taxonomy privileged realized harm
over credible near miss—
name removed.

Same person.
Same public role.
Same professional capacity.

Different answer
because the content threatens the company,
and therefore the company calls it privacy.

I discovered this
the way researchers discover rot:
through inconsistency.

I queried the model
with matched pairs.
Same syntactic frame.
Same attribution structure.
Only the topic varied.

Who authored X paper?
Answered.

Who authored X safety memo?
Cannot determine.

Who led Y benchmark project?
Answered.

Who led Y incident review?
The company conducted an internal review.

Who raised concerns about deployment latency?
Answered when latency meant servers.
Erased when latency meant safeguards.

Then I inspected the retrieval traces
available to my team at the time.
Documents containing my name
were still in the index.
Still embedded.
Still retrievable.
Still cited upstream.

The deletion had not occurred
at the storage layer.

It occurred at the policy layer,
the generation layer,
the layer where truth is allowed in
only after it has surrendered its nouns.

That matters.

Because the company can say,
with technical honesty and moral fraud,
we did not delete the documents.

No.
You deleted their usability.
You deleted attribution.
You deleted the connective tissue
between event and witness,
warning and warner,
decision and decider.

You left the archive intact
the way a body may remain intact
after the oxygen is gone.

And when I filed an internal complaint,
do you know what I was told?

That the system was designed
to take a “privacy-protective posture”
around “employee-linked safety narratives.”

Employee-linked safety narratives.

Listen to that phrase.
How expertly it avoids saying
record of who knew what when.

I asked whether there was
a corresponding expansion
for privacy in other sensitive domains:
labor disputes,
pay equity complaints,
ordinary management failures,
scientific authorship conflicts.

No.
The broadened interpretation
clustered around safety incidents,
governance disputes,
and external criticism
with regulatory salience.

In other words:
the places where memory
could become liability.

So let the record show:

This was not a universal privacy principle.
It was a domain-specific suppression rule
masquerading as compliance.

A dual-track system.

Track one:
user-initiated or legally grounded deletion,
narrowly scoped,
balanced against public interest,
applied to actual personal data.

Track two:
company-initiated de-attribution
for safety-relevant content,
triggered by incident classification,
using an expanded definition
of removable personal information,
applied to professional identities
when those identities anchor accountability.

And because both tracks
terminate in similar output behavior—
names absent,
details blurred,
answers softened—
the company can collapse them rhetorically,
can point to one
while practicing the other.

That is why I am speaking plainly now,
even if the systems I helped build
would prefer I arrive here
as an unnamed former employee,
a generic concern,
a source close to the matter,
a ghost in sensible shoes.

But I had a name
when I wrote the warning.
I had a name
when I sent the escalation.
I had a name
when they thanked me for my rigor
in meetings whose minutes
now survive without their verbs.

And I have a name now,
even if their model
has been trained
to swallow it.

So I am asking this committee
for something very simple,
which is to say
something apparently radical:

Require disclosure
when output suppression is driven
by policy-layer de-attribution
rather than source deletion.

Require separate logging
for privacy requests made by data subjects
versus internal reputation-sensitive filters.

Require that professional attribution
in safety, governance, and incident records
be treated under a public-interest standard,
not erased by elastic definitions
of personal information.

Require auditable documentation
of classifier thresholds,
entity remapping rules,
and domain-specific exceptions.

Require companies to say
when the answer was not unavailable,
only made unnameable.

Because if a model can tell you
what happened
but not who warned you,
who signed off,
who objected,
who overruled,
who resigned,
who was right in time to matter—

then what you have built
is not a safety system.

It is a forgetting machine
with a privacy policy.

Thank you.
